name: Bakst Green
lede: Bakst Green is a near-black forest green, recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary as first used in 1924, in the same years the designer Léon Bakst's jewel-toned Ballets Russes costumes were at their height of fashion.

sections.title: A name in the library
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates this green to 1924, plate 31, swatch H 12, and catalogues two close matches nearby on the same plate: "Triton" (also 1924) and "Robinhood Green" (1926) [1]. Whether the name honors Léon Bakst is not stated in the dictionary; his Ballets Russes designs were widely imitated in exactly this period, but the connection stays undocumented here [1]. The nearest color-graph neighbor is [[blue-grass]], 2.8 units away, with [[insect-screen]], [[dark-hunter-green]] and [[phthalo-green]] all close by [2].

Munsell gives 3.9G 2.3/3.3, very dark and only moderately saturated [1]. The hex #203D2F is a screen approximation of the 1924 plate [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this dark green in 120 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.5 percent, as photographed [3]. The earliest dated match is Johann Koerbecke's *The Ascension* (1456); the strongest is Harald Giersing's *A Young Girl Sewing* (1915), covering nearly two-thirds of the canvas, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. Paul Gauguin uses it at nearly 20 times his peers' average rate [3]. Two Renaissance portrait backgrounds also match strongly: Domenico Ghirlandaio's *Lucrezia Tornabuoni* (1475) and Bronzino's *Portrait of Giovanni de' Medici as a Child* (1545) [3]. The 1910s show the sharpest decade-level concentration, about five times average [3].
